name: Ankle and foot
pattern: Small, controlled ankle and foot movements: pointing and pulling up the foot, turning the sole in and out, circles, and toe work, often against a band.
setup: Sit on the floor or a chair with the leg straight or the heel on the floor.
For band work, loop the band around the forefoot and anchor it opposite the direction you will move.
Keep the knee and shin still; only the foot moves.

steps.text: Move the foot slowly to the end of the range against the band (up, down, in or out).
Return slowly over about 3 seconds, resisting the band.

cues.cue: Shin and knee still; only the foot turns.
cues.why: Rotating the leg hides the ankle motion you are training.

cues.cue: Train up, down, in and out.
cues.why: Four-way band strengthening improved strength, balance and hop tests in chronic ankle instability.
Eccentric control was part of the strength protocol that improved eversion strength.

cues.cue: For towel curls and foot activation, lift the arch without curling the toes hard.
cues.why: The small foot muscles support the arch and feed balance information.

cues.cue: 2-3 sets of 10-15, about 3 days a week.
cues.why: Supervised rehab exercise lowers the risk of another sprain.

tempo.note: About 2 s out, 1 s hold, 3 s back; 10-15 reps.

mistakes.name: Leg rolls instead of the ankle
mistakes.looks: For inversion or eversion the whole leg turns from the hip.
mistakes.fix: Hold the shin with a hand or pillow; move only the foot.
mistakes.why: The hip does the work and the ankle muscles get little load.

mistakes.name: Toes do the work
mistakes.looks: The toes claw hard while the ankle barely moves.
mistakes.fix: Relax the toes, lead with the whole foot.
mistakes.why: The long toe muscles take over from the ankle movers.

mistakes.name: Band snaps back
mistakes.looks: The foot is pulled back quickly by the band.
mistakes.why: Loses the eccentric half of the rep.

safety: Acute sprain: early gentle movement helps; start pain-free range work within a few days and see a clinician for a bad sprain.
Sharp pain, a pop, or you cannot put weight on the foot: get it checked.
Diabetes or poor foot sensation: check the skin under bands and towels.

variants.change: Band or cable adds load; anchor it opposite the movement.
Standing: body weight on the foot; harder and more like daily life.
Towel curl: pull a towel toward you with the toes, heel down.

subtypes.name: Ankle circles and alphabet
subtypes.change: Draw slow full circles with the foot, both directions.

subtypes.name: Band inversion and eversion
subtypes.change: Seated, heel down; turn the sole in (inversion, about 30°) or out (eversion, about 15°) against the band. ankleEv is eversion, + outward.

subtypes.name: Toe and arch work
subtypes.change: Seated or standing, heel down; spread, lift, press or curl the toes, or shorten the foot to lift the arch.

subtypes.name: Heel walk
subtypes.change: Walk on your heels with the toes pulled up high.

subtypes.name: Ankle stretches and rocks
subtypes.change: Kneel or half kneel and rock the knee forward over the toes (dorsiflexion), or sit back on the tops of the feet (plantar flexion). Hold or rock slowly.

motion.basis: Default: seated band dorsiflexion. Dorsiflexion and plantar flexion ranges from soucie2011 (adults 20-44: dorsiflexion about 13°, plantar flexion 55-62°); inversion and eversion ranges are common clinical norms (estimate). ankleEv (eversion, + outward) and toeFlex are extra keys not yet in the README convention; the rig needs a subtalar and toe joint for them. Protocol cues from hall2018, kaminski2013 and mckeon2015.
